one_liner: Header-only C++11 adaptive radix tree for C-string keys; 1.5-2.4x faster than std::map<std::string> in author's microbenchmark.
what_it_does: An in-memory ordered map from NUL-terminated byte strings to values, built as a university study implementation of Leis et al.'s Adaptive Radix Tree (the repo ships the author's report). It is not a drop-in container: the class art::art<T> exposes get/set/del on const char* keys, and get returns T{} when the key is absent while set and del return the previous value. It also has forward iterators via begin(), begin(key) (first key >= key) and end(), with it.key() rebuilding the key as a std::string. There is no size(), find, iterator-based erase or allocator parameter, and stored values are copied and never owned or freed by the tree.
how_it_is_fast: It is a byte-wise radix trie (8-bit span), so a lookup costs O(key length) byte steps instead of O(log n) full std::string comparisons down a red-black tree. Inner nodes adapt to their child count using the paper's Node4/Node16/Node48/Node256 layouts, which keeps nodes small and cache-friendly. On x86, Node16 is searched with SSE2 (_mm_cmpeq_epi8 + movemask + ctz); other architectures use a scalar binary search. Paths are compressed pessimistically: each node keeps its whole compressed path in a heap array, leaves keep the remaining key suffix, and matching uses std::mismatch. It omits the paper's hybrid 8-byte inline prefix, pointer tagging and concurrency, and nodes use virtual dispatch.
when_to_use: Single-threaded, in-memory ordered map with ASCII/text keys (decimal IDs, identifiers, paths) where std::map<std::string> insert/lookup is a measured hotspot and you still need sorted iteration.
Workloads around 1-2M keys with insert-heavy or mixed insert/delete traffic: the author's run shows about 2x over std::map on insert and mixed, and parity with std::unordered_map on insert.
Skewed (Zipf) lookups on short string keys, where it matched std::unordered_map (1.005x) while keeping keys ordered.
GPL-3.0-compatible projects, or as a small, readable reference ART (~1.75k lines of headers plus a written report) to study or adapt.
x86-64 Linux with GCC/Clang, the only configuration exercised by CI (ubuntu-22.04).
when_not_to_use: Pure point lookups or deletes with no need for ordering: in the same benchmark std::unordered_map was 1.9x faster on uniform lookups (230 vs 444 ns/op) and 1.45x faster on deletes.

Binary keys, keys containing NUL bytes, non-ASCII/UTF-8 keys, or native integer keys: the API is strlen-based and high bytes (>=0x80) are handled through signed-char arithmetic with several defective code paths (see gotchas).
Any concurrent use: the author's report says the implementation 'dictates single threaded usage'. There is no locking, OLC or ROWEX.

Production-critical or proprietary code: it is GPL-3.0, and serious bugs stayed open for years before being fixed in a Nov 2025 burst of PRs (node_16->node_48 growth made children unreachable, a one-byte overflow in set(), a crash iterating a single-element tree, an aarch64 crash). Node48/Node256 growth and shrink are not exercised by tree-level tests.

Memory-constrained deployments: every node carries a vtable pointer and a separately heap-allocated prefix. The repo publishes no memory comparison against std::map (make bench-mem profiles ART only).

integration.dependencies: none (doctest, picobench and a zipf generator are git submodules used only by tests/benchmarks)
integration.min_toolchain: C++11 (CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 11); CMake 3.12 for the bundled build. Uses GCC/Clang builtins (__builtin_ctz) on x86. Supported compiler versions are not documented.
integration.platforms: x86/x86-64 (SSE2 Node16 path, CI on ubuntu-22.04). Other architectures fall back to scalar code but need -fsigned-char (Linux aarch64 crashed per issue #17). Windows/MSVC not documented or tested.
integration.thread_safety: Not thread-safe: the author's report states single-threaded usage and there is no internal synchronization. get() is const and non-mutating, so concurrent readers with no writer look safe from code reading, but that is not documented.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — it replaces std::map<std::string,T> for ordered string-keyed storage, but the API differs (get/set/del on const char*, T{} for missing keys, no size/find/erase(iterator)/allocator, iterator operator* returns T by value), and the ordering differs for bytes >= 0x80.

gotchas: Assumes signed char: Node48/Node256 index with 128 + partial_key. The aarch64 fix (issue #17) only adds -fsigned-char to this project's CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS and is not exported by the INTERFACE target, so your own code on unsigned-char targets must add -fsigned-char. Even then, iteration order puts bytes 0x80-0xFF before ASCII, unlike std::map<std::string>, which compares as unsigned char.

Keys are C strings: "aa" and "aa\0" are the same key (a test documents this after issue #21). prefix_len_ is uint16_t, so keys of 64 KiB or more would be truncated (from code reading). Because get() returns T{} for a missing key, art<int> cannot tell 0 from absent, so store pointers or a sentinel-bearing type.

art has a raw root pointer and a destructor but no user-defined or deleted copy operations, so copying a tree (for example passing it by value) makes a shallow copy and a double free (from code reading). del() and ~art() never free stored values, so pointer values are yours to manage.

Code-reading defects in untested paths (not executed here):
- node_256::shrink loops partial_key 0..255 over children_[128+k], which reads past the array and skips bytes >=0x80.
- node_48 grow/shrink loops stop at 126 and drop a child keyed 0x7F.
- del() finds the lone sibling with next_partial_key(0) and can throw std::out_of_range when that sibling's byte is >=0x80.
- begin(key) hits `continue` without advancing when the seek key sorts below a leaf's suffix, e.g. tree {"b"} with begin("a"), which looks like an infinite loop.
- begin() on an empty tree dereferences a null root.
Tests cover only decimal/hex keys and seeks to keys already in the tree.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: The catalogued siblings are learned indexes over sorted numeric keys benchmarked against STX B+-tree (CARMI, PGM-index) and persistent on-disk KV engines (libmdbx, redb, TerarkDB). Pick this ART when you need a mutable, in-process, in-memory ordered map keyed by variable-length text strings and can accept GPL-3.0; pick PGM/CARMI for mostly static numeric key sets and a sibling KV store when you need durability.
verified_claims_summary: The author's picobench table (README, Nov 2018) was built with CMake Release -O3 -DNDEBUG; compiler, standard library and CPU are not stated. It ran 1.6M operations on random 64-bit (insert/delete) or 32-bit (query) integers formatted as decimal strings, with key-string construction inside every timed loop. Against std::map<std::string,int>, ART was 1.5x faster on uniform lookups, about 2x on insert/delete/mixed and 2.4x on base-64-encoded keys, while std::unordered_map beat ART by 1.4-1.9x on lookups and deletes. An earlier 16M-key run (Oct 2018 README, older code) showed smaller margins on delete (1.07x) and insert (1.65x), and the README heading still says '16M keys'. The numbers predate the Nov 2025 correctness fixes.
status_note: Dormant from June 2022 until a Nov 2025 burst of mostly Copilot-agent bug-fix PRs and release 6.0 (last commit 2025-11-24, 0 open issues, 174 stars); header-only and small enough to vendor into GPL-3.0 code, but treat it as study-grade rather than a hardened production container.
